title: When Decisions You Dont Agree With Come Down From Above
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece addresses a recurring leadership dilemma: how to represent a decision made above you that you personally disagree with. The author rejects both extremes — hiding disagreement entirely and undermining the decision by openly aligning with the team against it — in favor of a specific rhetorical move: acknowledging disagreement briefly without dwelling on it, then committing fully and convincingly to executing the decision because the leader genuinely accepts their obligation to the larger organization. The essay frames this obligation as core to what leadership actually is, arguing that a leader who positions themselves as separate from 'they' (the organization) teaches their own team to do the same. It closes by connecting this discipline to the well-known principle of 'disagree and commit.'
points: The essay's key move is precise, not just about attitude: acknowledge disagreement briefly and without elaboration, then commit with genuine conviction, avoiding both suppression and open undermining.

It identifies a structural leadership definition — the leader is always part of the organizational 'They,' even while leading a team that calls itself 'We' — as the philosophical basis for the obligation.
It traces a specific downstream consequence of failing this discipline: a team that watches its leader distance themselves from decisions learns that disagreement-as-defiance is normal.
It ties the practice to the well-known 'disagree and commit' principle, giving the argument an established vocabulary leaders may already recognize.
quotes: Should the leader be transparent in their opposition to the decision but tell the team they must execute it anyway? Or should they engage as if the decision is their own and risk alienating the team and losing their respect?
Unless the decision is unethical, immoral, or illegal, the obligation of any leader in the organization is to support it as if it were their own.

The team can learn, if it doesn’t already know, that the decision is not one a leader agrees with. Once that is out in the open but not elaborated on, good leaders make a strong pitch that they are 100 percent behind executing the decision.
We” versus “They” doesn’t come up for one important reason: the Leader is always part of the “They,” even when they represent a specific team that prides itself as “We.
Disagreement is one thing. Commitment after disagreement is another.
